summary: The Port Control Protocol lets hosts ask a NAT or firewall to open or map ports. This standards-track RFC reserves one well-known IPv4 address and one well-known IPv6 address as PCP anycast addresses, so a client can reach its nearest PCP-aware middlebox without first learning that device's address some other way.

eli5.summary: Normally you need to know a helper's phone number before calling. This sets aside one special number everyone can dial, and the closest helper picks up.

questions: how does a pcp client find the nat
what is the pcp anycast address
subtitle: Two well-known addresses let a client find its nearest NAT or firewall without being told where it is.

tldr.problem: A PCP client needs to know the address of the NAT or firewall it should talk to. The default router is only right in simple networks, and configuration files or DHCP options can be hard to keep correct in larger ones.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC reserves one IPv4 and one IPv6 anycast address for PCP servers. Clients try them after the default router, and the closest PCP-aware device on the path answers.
tldr.outcome: Clients can reach an upstream middlebox such as a Carrier-Grade NAT with no extra discovery machinery, though parallel firewalls with asymmetric routing and possible leakage need care.

today: RFC 7723 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the document that defines the PCP anycast addresses.

sections.title: Why PCP Needs a Well-Known Address
sections.content:
The Port Control Protocol (PCP, RFC 6887) lets a host control how upstream devices such as NAT64, NAT44 and firewalls forward incoming packets. The base protocol defines the message formats, but the address a client sends to is assumed to be the default router, or has to come from a configuration file or a DHCP option (RFC 7291).

This document takes a different approach and establishes two well-known anycast addresses for the PCP server, one IPv4 and one IPv6. Clients usually send requests there if no other PCP server address is known, or after attempts to other addresses have failed. Implementations should still offer a way to disable or override these addresses, such as a configuration file option.
sections.eli5: Instead of asking every house for its own phone number, everyone agrees on one number to call for help. Whoever is nearest answers.

sections.title: When Anycast Beats the Default Router
sections.content:
Anycast is most useful in larger networks. If the PCP-enabled NAT or firewall is not on the client's default gateway but further upstream in a Carrier-Grade NAT (CGN), sending PCP requests to the gateway will not work. A configuration file or DHCP server would have to mirror the topology and the router and CGN setup, which may be cumbersome to maintain.

With several upstream CGNs and a dynamic routing protocol such as OSPF, that approach may not be feasible at all, because it cannot say in time which CGN to talk to. An anycast request just travels through the network like any other packet until a PCP-capable device receives it and replies. The address can also be hard-coded into an application, so no API is needed to pass the DHCP-learned server address up from the operating system.
sections.eli5: If the right helper keeps changing, a list of phone numbers goes out of date. One shared number always reaches whoever is closest right now.

sections.title: Client and Server Behavior
sections.content:
A PCP client can add the anycast addresses, after the default router list for IPv4 and IPv6, to its list of PCP servers (step 2 in Section 8.1 of RFC 6887). The list is then processed as specified in RFC 7488. To use only the anycast address, put it in the configuration file or DHCP option.

PCP servers can be configured to listen on the anycast addresses. When a server receives a request destined for an anycast address it supports, it sends the reply using that same anycast address as the source address.
sections.eli5: The client calls the shared number only after trying the usual ones. The helper who answers replies using that same shared number, so the client knows who is talking.

sections.title: Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC points to RFC 4786 for operating anycast services and RFC 7094 for architecture. It warns that anycast has limits in some networks, which other discovery methods such as DHCP or a configuration file can cover.

The main example is a network connected upstream through several parallel firewalls, each with its own PCP server. Only one server receives a given client's messages, depending on routing tables. If routing is symmetric, this works. If a routing change moves the client to a different server, the client sees it like a PCP server reboot and can detect it through the Epoch field in the next response or ANNOUNCE message, then re-establish its rules.

With asymmetric routing, rules set in only one firewall will not give bidirectional connectivity. One approach is an implementation-specific mechanism that synchronizes state among all border firewalls, so a PEER message to any one sets rules in all. Another is to use DHCP or a configuration file to learn every PCP server and configure each. Anycast reaches only the closest upstream server, but it may be combined with the PCP proxy function (RFC 7648) for cascaded NATs or firewalls.
sections.eli5: If two doors lead out of a building and a letter goes through one but the reply comes back through the other, the plan breaks. Then you need the doors to share notes, or to tell each door separately.

sections.title: The Registered Addresses
sections.content:
IANA assigned a single IPv4 address, 192.0.0.9/32, from the 192.0.0.0/24 prefix, and a single IPv6 address, 2001:1::1/128, from the 2001:0000::/23 prefix. Both are registered as special-purpose addresses (RFC 6890) under the name Port Control Protocol Anycast, with an allocation date of October 2015 and no termination date.

In both registries the Source, Destination, Forwardable and Global values are True, and Reserved-by-Protocol is False.
sections.eli5: Like a city picking one official number for the fire station, one version for each kind of phone network.

sections.title: Leakage and Hijacking
sections.content:
If a network has no border gateway, NAT or firewall aware of the anycast address, outgoing PCP requests could leak onto the Internet and reveal information about internal devices. Because the address is IANA-assigned and well known, border gateways can block such packets, and routers in the default-free zone should drop them. Sensitive clients can set an IP TTL to limit how far requests travel, though choosing the value is out of scope. Before sending privacy-sensitive parameters, a client can send an ANNOUNCE request without parameters to check that a PCP server handles the anycast address.

Hosts treat anycast addresses as normal unicast, so hijacking in the first segment needs the attacker to impersonate the default router, for example by ARP spoofing. Further in, routing protocols such as OSPF or BGP could be abused with counterfeit announcements. PCP authentication (RFC 7652) may help, but its setup effort can defeat fully automatic configuration, so the RFC recommends weighing its costs and benefits per scenario.
sections.eli5: A call meant for a nearby helper could end up with a stranger far away, so the network should block those calls from leaving, and you can first check someone really is listening.
